questions.stem: In the catabolism of CTP:

options.label: A
options.text: uric acid is an end product.

options.label: B
options.text: nitrogen will be released in the form of ammonia (ammonium ion).

options.label: C
options.text: the nitrogen-containing ring will be oxidized.

options.label: D
options.text: the final product will have the same type of nitrogen-containing ring as CTP.

questions.why: Cytidine nucleotides are degraded through pyrimidine pathways. Deamination releases amino nitrogen, present mainly as ammonium at physiological pH. The remaining pyrimidine ring can then be reduced and opened during degradation.

notes.A: Uric acid is the end product of human purine degradation. CTP contains a pyrimidine base and follows a different pathway.
notes.C: Pyrimidine breakdown involves reduction and opening of the ring rather than simple oxidation of an intact ring.
notes.D: The pyrimidine ring is opened and degraded to smaller compounds. It is not retained in the final catabolic products.
notes.E: Hypoxanthine is an intermediate in purine metabolism and does not arise from the pyrimidine ring of CTP.

questions.stem: The formation of dATP for DNA synthesis occurs primarily by:

options.label: A
options.text: de novo synthesis beginning with dPRPP.

options.label: C
options.text: salvaging adenine using a nucleoside phosphorylase and dR 1-P.

options.label: D
options.text: converting ADP to dADP using thioredoxin.

options.label: E
options.text: converting dIMP to dAMP using 5,10-methylene THF.

questions.why: Ribonucleotide reductase converts ADP to dADP using reducing equivalents provided by thioredoxin or a related system. Nucleoside diphosphate kinase can then phosphorylate dADP to dATP for DNA synthesis.

notes.A: De novo purine synthesis begins with ribose-containing PRPP. The deoxyribose is generated later by ribonucleotide reduction.
notes.B: Adenine phosphoribosyltransferase salvages adenine to AMP, a ribonucleotide. That reaction does not directly supply dATP.
notes.C: A phosphorylase may participate in nucleoside salvage, but ADP reduction is the major route to the deoxyadenosine nucleotide pool.
notes.E: Methylene-tetrahydrofolate provides a one-carbon unit for thymidylate synthesis, not the principal route from a purine intermediate to dATP.

questions.stem: Which of the following would NOT be expected to contribute to hyperuricemia (gout)?

options.label: C
options.text: Unusually high turnover of nucleic acids

questions.why: Xanthine oxidase carries out the final oxidation steps from hypoxanthine and xanthine to urate. Inhibiting it decreases urate formation, which is why its inhibitors can be used to lower urate in gout.

notes.A: Elevated PRPP can increase de novo purine synthesis, providing more purines that can eventually be degraded to urate.
notes.C: High nucleic acid turnover releases more purine substrates for degradation and can raise urate levels.
notes.D: Adenosine deaminase produces inosine that can enter the hypoxanthine-to-urate pathway. It does not block urate formation.
notes.E: HGPRT normally salvages hypoxanthine and guanine. Deficiency favours purine degradation and can increase de novo synthesis.

questions.stem: The major control of de novo pyrimidine nucleotide synthesis in man is:

options.label: E
options.text: feedback inhibition of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II.

questions.why: In human cells, the carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II domain of CAD controls entry to de novo pyrimidine synthesis. Pyrimidine nucleotides such as UTP provide feedback inhibition, while PRPP can stimulate activity.

notes.A: Glutamine–PRPP amidotransferase regulates de novo purine synthesis, rather than synthesis of the pyrimidine ring.
notes.B: Aspartate transcarbamylase is a classic regulatory enzyme in some bacteria. Human pathway feedback acts chiefly at the carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II activity of CAD.
notes.C: N-acetylglutamate activates mitochondrial carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I, which supplies the urea cycle.
notes.D: Substrate availability can influence flux, but feedback at carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II is the characteristic control mechanism in this comparison.

questions.stem: Aspartate plays a role in all of the following EXCEPT:

options.label: C
options.text: de novo synthesis of orotic acid.

options.label: D
options.text: maintenance of the adenine nucleotide pool by a salvage mechanism.

questions.why: CTP synthetase converts UTP to CTP by adding amino nitrogen from glutamine. Aspartate participates in synthesis of the pyrimidine ring and contributes nitrogen at other steps, including conversion of IMP toward AMP.

notes.B: IMP is converted to adenylosuccinate using aspartate before fumarate is released to give AMP.
notes.C: Aspartate contributes atoms to the pyrimidine ring that is eventually present in orotate.
notes.D: Salvaged hypoxanthine can form IMP, which can be converted to AMP using aspartate. Direct salvage of adenine to AMP is a separate route.
notes.E: Aspartate is one of the standard amino acid residues incorporated into proteins during translation.

questions.stem: Allopurinol is an inhibitor of xanthine oxidase. Administration of allopurinol to a patient with gout and normal HG-PRT levels would be expected to lead to all of the following EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: decreased de novo synthesis of IMP.

options.label: C
options.text: an increase of hypoxanthine in the blood.

questions.why: Allopurinol decreases urate formation by inhibiting xanthine oxidase, allowing upstream purines to accumulate. With functioning HGPRT, enhanced hypoxanthine salvage consumes PRPP, so an increase in PRPP is not the expected effect.

notes.A: Increased salvage can consume PRPP and replenish IMP, both of which can suppress de novo purine synthesis.
notes.B: Inhibiting the last steps of urate synthesis decreases production and typically lowers urinary urate excretion.
notes.C: Hypoxanthine is upstream of the blocked oxidation steps and may accumulate, with some diverted into salvage.
notes.E: Xanthine cannot be oxidised to urate as efficiently during inhibition, so its concentration or excretion can rise.

questions.stem:
Direct sources of purine ring atoms in the de novo synthesis of IMP include:
1. glutamine.
2. a component of the tetrahydrofolate one-carbon pool.
3. aspartate.
4. glycine.
questions.why: The purine ring of IMP receives atoms from glycine, glutamine, aspartate and formyl-tetrahydrofolate. Bicarbonate contributes another carbon. These atoms are assembled on the activated ribose provided by PRPP.

notes.A: Glutamine, formyl-tetrahydrofolate and aspartate contribute ring atoms. Glycine also supplies two carbons and one nitrogen.
notes.B: Glutamine and aspartate provide nitrogen, but glycine and formyl groups are also needed to build the purine ring.
notes.C: The one-carbon donor and glycine supply several atoms. Aspartate and glutamine also contribute nitrogen.
notes.D: Glycine supplies three ring atoms. It is joined by contributions from other nitrogen donors and one-carbon units.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a purine nucleotide?
questions.why: AMP contains adenine, a purine base with a fused two-ring structure. The other listed nucleotides contain the single-ring pyrimidines uracil, cytosine or thymine.

notes.B: Uridine monophosphate contains uracil, which is a pyrimidine base.
notes.C: Uridine triphosphate has three phosphate groups but its base remains the pyrimidine uracil.
notes.D: Cytidine triphosphate contains cytosine, a pyrimidine.
notes.E: Thymidine monophosphate contains thymine, a pyrimidine commonly found in DNA.

questions.stem:
In eukaryotes the enzymes involved are on the following proteins:
I. CAD protein has activities of enzymes for the de novo biosynthesis of dihydro-orotate
II. the second protein is a complex dehydrogenase located in the inner mitochondrial membrane with its active site facing the cytosol
III. the third protein has activity of only orotate phosphoribosyl transferase
questions.why: All three statements are true regarding the eukaryotic enzymes.

notes.A: Leaves out II and III, which are also true.
notes.B: Leaves out III, which is also true.
notes.C: Leaves out I, which is also true.
notes.D: Leaves out II, which is also true.

questions.stem:
Consider the following about Azaserine:
I. It is a structural analogue of glutamine
II. It inhibits the activity of aspartate transcarbamoylase
III. It inhibits the activity of QP synthetase
questions.why: Azaserine is a glutamine analog that inhibits glutamine-requiring enzymes like QP synthetase, but not ATCase.

notes.A: Leaves out III, which is also true.
notes.B: Includes II, which is false, and leaves out III, which is true.
notes.C: Includes II, which is false, and leaves out I, which is true.
notes.E: Includes II, which is false.

questions.stem:
Orotic aciduria is associated with:
I. deficiency of both orotate phosphoribosyl transferase and orotidylate decarboxylase
II. deficiency of dihydroorotate dehydrogenase
III. deficiency of aspartate transcarbamoylase
questions.why: Hereditary orotic aciduria results from deficient UMP synthase, a bifunctional enzyme with orotate phosphoribosyltransferase and orotidine monophosphate decarboxylase activities. Impaired utilisation of orotate allows it to accumulate.

notes.B: Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase makes orotate upstream. Its deficiency is not the classic cause of an inability to convert orotate to UMP.
notes.C: The two UMPS activities explain hereditary orotate accumulation. The listed upstream enzymes do not account for that classic defect.
notes.D: Aspartate transcarbamylase acts before orotate is formed and is not the enzyme deficient in classic hereditary orotic aciduria.
notes.E: The disorder involves the bifunctional UMP synthase step. Neither of the other enzyme defects is part of its defining mechanism.

questions.stem:
Consider the following:
I. HGPRT is involved in the salvage synthesis of IMP or GMP
II. deficiency of HGPRT may lead to gout
III. severe deficiency of HGPRT may lead to severe mental retardation
questions.why: HGPRT salvages hypoxanthine and guanine by producing IMP and GMP, respectively. Deficiency increases urate production and can cause gout. Severe loss causes Lesch–Nyhan disease with prominent neurological and behavioural manifestations.

notes.A: Salvage is the enzyme's key reaction, but the associated overproduction of urate and neurological phenotype are also recognised.
notes.B: Loss of salvage and gout are related. Severe deficiency also affects central nervous system function.
notes.C: Gout and neurological findings can occur. HGPRT normally salvages purine bases into IMP or GMP.
notes.D: The salvage reaction and severe neurological features are correct. Excess urate can also give rise to gout.

questions.stem: Building blocks of nucleic acids are
questions.why: Nucleic acids are polymers of nucleotides. Each unit includes a nitrogenous base, a sugar and phosphate. Phosphodiester bonds connect the sugar–phosphate backbone.

notes.B: A nucleoside has a base and sugar but lacks phosphate. Phosphorylated units supply the building blocks for the backbone.
notes.C: Amino acids are joined by peptide bonds to form proteins, rather than nucleic acids.
notes.D: Histones are proteins that bind and package DNA. They are not the repeating chemical units of DNA.

questions.stem: An important similarity between the activities of DNA polymerases and RNA polymerases is the:

options.label: D
options.text: 3' to 5' copying of a template strand.

questions.why: Both DNA and RNA polymerases read the template in the 3′-to-5′ direction. They extend the new strand at its 3′ end, so the newly synthesised chain grows in the 5′-to-3′ direction.

notes.A: DNA polymerases use deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates. RNA polymerases instead use ribonucleoside triphosphates.
notes.B: Replicative DNA polymerases require a primer with a free 3′ hydroxyl group. Cellular RNA polymerases can generally start a transcript without a primer.
notes.C: A promoter is where transcription is initiated. Replication is initiated at origins with separate priming steps.

questions.stem: Which of the following is true about DNA polymerase?

options.label: A
options.text: It can synthesize DNA in the 3'to 5'direction

options.label: B
options.text: It can synthesize DNA in the 5'to 3'direction

options.label: C
options.text: It can synthesize mRNA in the 3'to 5'direction

options.label: D
options.text: It can synthesize mRNA in the 5'to 3'direction

questions.why: DNA polymerase adds each incoming deoxyribonucleotide to the free 3′ hydroxyl group of the growing DNA strand. This produces net synthesis in the 5′-to-3′ direction.

notes.A: The template is read 3′ to 5′, and some proofreading also operates in that direction. DNA synthesis itself proceeds 5′ to 3′.
notes.C: Messenger RNA is made by RNA polymerase, which also extends a product in the 5′-to-3′ direction.
notes.D: RNA synthesis proceeds 5′ to 3′, but the catalyst that makes mRNA is RNA polymerase rather than DNA polymerase.

questions.stem: What is the reaction in DNA replication catalyzed by DNA ligase?

options.label: A
options.text: Addition of new nucleotides to the leading strand

options.label: B
options.text: Addition of new nucleotide to the lagging strand

options.label: C
options.text: Formation of a phosphodiester bond between the 3'-OH of one Okazaki fragment and the 5'-phosphate of the next on the lagging strand

options.label: D
options.text: Base pairing of the template and the newly formed DNA strand

questions.why: DNA ligase seals a nick in the DNA backbone by joining an adjacent 3′ hydroxyl group and 5′ phosphate. During lagging-strand replication this joins DNA fragments after removal and replacement of RNA primers.

notes.A: Leading-strand extension is performed by DNA polymerase, which adds new nucleotides to a growing chain.
notes.B: DNA polymerase synthesises the lagging-strand fragments. Ligase then joins the adjacent backbone ends.
notes.D: Complementary base pairing specifies the sequence of the new strand. Ligase acts on a break in the sugar–phosphate backbone.

questions.stem: Which of the following reactions is required for proofreading during DNA replication by DNA polymerase III?
questions.why: The proofreading activity of bacterial DNA polymerase III removes a mismatched nucleotide from the growing 3′ end. It is a 3′-to-5′ exonuclease activity, after which synthesis can resume.

notes.A: A 5′-to-3′ exonuclease acts at a different end. In bacteria such an activity is associated with primer removal by DNA polymerase I.
notes.C: An endonuclease cleaves within a strand. Proofreading removes a nucleotide from the end of the newly synthesised strand.
notes.D: Proofreading does not require an internal cut in the template. It requires exonucleolytic removal from the 3′ end of the product.

questions.stem: Which of the following enzymes remove supercoiling in replicating DNA ahead of the replication fork?
questions.why: Unwinding at a replication fork can generate positive supercoils ahead of it. Topoisomerases relieve this torsional stress through controlled breakage and resealing of DNA strands.

notes.A: DNA polymerases synthesise complementary DNA. They do not provide the principal mechanism for relieving supercoiling ahead of a fork.
notes.B: Helicases separate the parental strands, which can generate torsional stress farther ahead. Topoisomerases relieve that stress.
notes.C: Primases synthesise short RNA primers that provide starting points for DNA synthesis.

questions.stem: DNA unwinding is done by
questions.why: Helicase uses energy to separate complementary DNA strands at the replication fork. This exposes single-stranded templates for DNA polymerases and other components of the replication machinery.

notes.A: DNA ligase seals breaks in the sugar–phosphate backbone. It does not separate paired strands.
notes.C: Topoisomerases relieve torsional strain produced during unwinding. Helicase opens the double helix at the fork.
notes.D: Nucleases cleave nucleic acid bonds. Strand separation during ordinary replication does not require digestion of the DNA backbone.

questions.stem: Which of the following process does not occur in prokaryotes
questions.why: Prokaryotes do not undergo RNA splicing.

notes.A: Prokaryotes replicate DNA.
notes.B: Prokaryotes transcribe genes.
notes.C: Prokaryotes translate mRNA.

questions.stem: Termination of replication is triggered by
questions.why: In the classical model for Escherichia coli, Tus binds Ter sites and stops a replication fork approaching from the nonpermissive direction. The opposing forks then complete replication in the terminus region. Other organisms can use different termination mechanisms.

notes.A: DNA polymerase elongates the new strands. It is not the sequence-specific fork barrier in the Tus–Ter system.
notes.B: Helicase separates the parental strands. In the Tus–Ter system its progression is blocked at a termination site.
notes.C: Single-strand binding protein stabilises exposed DNA during replication. It does not recognise Ter sites to stop the fork.

questions.stem: A piece of double stranded DNA has 30% A, what will be the % of G?
questions.why: For double-stranded DNA, adenine pairs with thymine and guanine pairs with cytosine. If adenine and thymine each make up 30 percent, the remaining 40 percent is split equally between guanine and cytosine.

notes.A: Adenine and thymine have equal proportions. Guanine pairs with cytosine and need not match adenine's percentage.
notes.B: Forty percent is the combined proportion of guanine and cytosine, rather than guanine alone.
notes.D: Seventy percent is the portion made of bases other than adenine, including thymine and cytosine.
notes.E: Base pairing supplies the required relationships for the percentages in an ordinary double-stranded DNA molecule.

questions.stem: You have a piece of DNA with the sequence ATGC. From this you know,

options.label: C
options.text: A could be at either the 5' end or the 3' end of DNA

questions.why: Without explicit labels, 'A' could technically be at either end.

notes.A: Without labels, the orientation is unknown.
notes.B: Without labels, the orientation is unknown.
notes.D: ATGC read on the other strand is GCAT, so it is not palindromic.
notes.E: Option C is correct.

questions.stem: Genomic DNA is resulting in the production of
questions.why: Transcription uses genomic DNA as a template for an RNA product. A protein-coding gene generates an mRNA or precursor transcript. Translation of the mRNA is a later step.

notes.B: Transfer RNA is transcribed from its genes. It is an adaptor used during translation, rather than a translation product.
notes.C: Transcription produces RNA. New genomic DNA is made during DNA replication.
notes.D: Translation makes protein from mRNA. It does not read genomic DNA directly.
notes.E: Replication copies genomic DNA to DNA. Messenger RNA is produced by transcription.

questions.stem: ___ is the adaptor that is key to converting the triplet codons of mRNA into the protein polymers.
questions.why: Transfer RNA carries an amino acid and presents an anticodon that pairs with a codon in mRNA. Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases attach the correct amino acid, allowing the ribosome to translate the codon into a residue in the growing protein.

notes.B: Ribosomal RNA helps form the ribosome and contributes to peptide bond catalysis. It does not carry a separate amino acid for each codon.
notes.C: Messenger RNA supplies the sequence of codons. Transfer RNA links each codon to its corresponding amino acid.
notes.D: Small interfering RNA helps direct sequence-specific gene silencing. It is not the adaptor carrying amino acids during translation.
notes.E: The standard amino acid-bearing adaptor is a transfer RNA with a codon-recognising anticodon.

questions.stem: In eukaryotes, which of the following DNA polymerase is required for mitochondrial DNA replication?
questions.why: DNA polymerase gamma is the principal replicative polymerase for eukaryotic mitochondrial DNA. The polymerase and other components of the mitochondrial replication machinery are encoded by nuclear genes and imported into mitochondria.

notes.A: Polymerase alpha works with primase to initiate DNA synthesis during nuclear chromosome replication.
notes.B: Polymerase beta is best known for base excision repair, rather than as the principal mitochondrial replicative polymerase.
notes.D: Polymerase delta is a major nuclear replicative polymerase and is not the principal enzyme duplicating mitochondrial DNA.

questions.stem: During replication, Okazaki fragments elongate

options.label: A
options.text: leading strand towards the replication fork

options.label: B
options.text: lagging strand towards the replication fork

options.label: C
options.text: leading strand away from the replication fork

options.label: D
options.text: lagging strand away from the replication fork

questions.why: DNA polymerase always extends a strand in the 5′-to-3′ direction. On the lagging strand, this makes each Okazaki fragment grow away from the moving fork, even though new fragments begin near the fork.

notes.A: The leading strand is usually copied continuously in the direction of fork movement. It does not normally consist of Okazaki fragments.
notes.B: New lagging-strand fragments start near the fork, but each is extended away from it.
notes.C: The leading strand extends toward the fork, while discontinuous synthesis occurs on the lagging strand.

questions.stem: A disorganized, generally encapsulated mass that does not invade adjacent tissue is known as a...
questions.why: A benign tumour is a localised neoplasm that does not invade nearby tissue or metastasise. Many benign tumours are circumscribed or encapsulated, though a capsule is not required for the diagnosis.

notes.A: Neoplasia is abnormal new growth and can be benign or malignant. The lack of invasion identifies the more specific term here.
notes.C: Anaplasia describes loss of differentiation and is often associated with aggressive malignancy, rather than a localised benign mass.
notes.D: Cancer refers to a malignant neoplasm with the capacity for invasion, which the stem excludes.
notes.E: Angiogenesis is formation of new blood vessels. It can occur around growths but does not name a type of mass.

questions.stem: The inducer exhibits positive control by binding to a ___ molecule, ___ the process of transcription.
questions.why: Inducer binds repressor, causing it to fall off, increasing transcription.

notes.A: The operator is DNA, and the inducer binds the repressor.
notes.B: The inducer increases transcription.
notes.D: Removing the repressor increases transcription.
notes.E: Co-repressors help repressors bind, decreasing transcription.

questions.stem: Catabolism of alternative sugar sources is repressed, cAMP levels are low, RNA pol is not recruited, and the lac operon is not transcribed in the presence of:
questions.why: In the standard lac operon model, plentiful glucose keeps bacterial cAMP low. The cAMP–CAP activator complex then forms less readily, so recruitment of RNA polymerase and expression of the operon are reduced.

notes.A: Insulin is an animal hormone and is not the carbohydrate signal acting on the bacterial lac system.
notes.B: Glucagon is a vertebrate hormone regulating nutrient metabolism. It is not the bacterial signal that lowers cAMP in this model.
notes.C: Glycogen is a carbohydrate store. The classic catabolite repression signal here is readily available glucose.
notes.E: Lactose can give rise to allolactose, which relieves repression by LacI. Glucose can still reduce expression through the cAMP–CAP pathway.

questions.stem: Attenuation of transcription of the Trp operon occurs with ___ levels of Trp, exhibiting ___ control.
questions.why: At high tryptophan availability, charged tryptophan tRNA allows rapid translation of the bacterial leader peptide. This favours an RNA terminator and premature cessation of transcription, decreasing expression of the tryptophan synthesis genes.

notes.B: High tryptophan favours attenuation, but attenuation decreases expression and therefore acts as negative control.
notes.C: At low tryptophan, translation can stall at the leader's tryptophan codons. This favours transcription continuing rather than terminating early.
notes.D: Low tryptophan relieves attenuation. The attenuation mechanism itself reduces transcription when tryptophan is abundant.
notes.E: Availability of tryptophan changes the response through charged tRNA and leader translation. The standard comparison is between high and low availability.

questions.stem: Which of the following involves regulating the assembly of the transcription complex containing the RNA pol and its binding to the TATA box and the promoter?
questions.why: Control of RNA polymerase recruitment and preinitiation complex assembly regulates whether transcription begins. Changes at a core promoter such as a TATA-containing promoter therefore occur at the transcriptional level.

notes.B: Post-transcriptional regulation acts on RNA after it is made, for example by changing processing or stability.
notes.C: Translational regulation controls production of protein from an existing mRNA, often by affecting ribosome recruitment.
notes.D: Post-translational control acts on a protein after synthesis, for example through a chemical modification that changes activity.

questions.stem: The genetic change that produced the mutant hemoglobin in sickle cell anemia can be classified as which type of mutation?
questions.why: The HbS variant replaces glutamate with valine at the sixth amino acid of the mature beta-globin chain. A substitution that changes the amino acid encoded by a codon is a missense mutation.

notes.A: A silent mutation changes the DNA sequence without changing the amino acid encoded. HbS has an amino acid replacement.
notes.C: A nonsense mutation creates a premature stop codon. This variant instead produces a full-length chain with one residue changed.
notes.D: No extra nucleotide is inserted in the classic HbS mutation. One nucleotide substitution changes the codon.
notes.E: The mutation does not remove a nucleotide or beta-globin residue. It changes the identity of one amino acid.

questions.stem: Which of the following enzymes are NOT used in cDNA cloning?
questions.why: Complementary DNA is made from an RNA template by reverse transcriptase, not by RNA polymerase. RNA polymerase produces RNA, so it is not the enzyme required to copy the RNA into DNA in the standard comparison.

notes.B: Reverse transcriptase is an RNA-dependent DNA polymerase and can make a DNA copy of the RNA.
notes.C: Some traditional cloning designs use restriction endonucleases to cut DNA at defined sites. Other designs can use different assembly methods.
notes.D: DNA ligase can join compatible DNA ends in traditional cloning. Its role is distinct from copying an RNA template.
notes.E: DNA polymerase activity can be used during completion of a double-stranded cDNA molecule.

questions.stem: The process in which mRNA is converted to cDNA is called
questions.why: Reverse transcription is synthesis of DNA using RNA as a template. When the starting material is mRNA, the resulting complementary DNA represents the RNA sequence.

notes.A: Ordinary transcription uses DNA as the template and produces RNA, the opposite direction of information transfer.
notes.C: Translation reads messenger RNA to make a polypeptide. It does not make a DNA copy.
notes.D: Replication uses DNA as a template to produce DNA. Reverse transcription instead starts with RNA.
notes.E: Splicing joins RNA segments after removal of introns. The product remains RNA rather than becoming DNA.

questions.stem: A gene for insulin has been inserted into a vector for obtaining its protein product only. Such a vector is called
questions.why: An expression vector is designed to allow a carried gene to be expressed in a host. The purpose in this question is to produce the encoded protein, rather than simply to store a copy of the DNA sequence.

notes.B: The stated objective is expression of the protein. A vector used to reduce expression serves a different purpose.
notes.C: A genomic-library vector is used primarily to maintain DNA fragments as a collection, which does not by itself ensure protein expression.
notes.D: A vector designed to produce the protein from an inserted gene has a recognised name, an expression vector.

questions.stem: Which of the following is true of both eukaryotic and prokaryotic gene expression?

options.label: A
options.text: After transcription, a 3' poly A tail and a 5' cap are added to mRNA

options.label: B
options.text: Translation of mRNA can begin before transcription is complete

options.label: C
options.text: mRNA is synthesized in the 3' to 5' direction

options.label: D
options.text: RNA polymerase binds at a promoter region upstream to the gene

options.label: E
options.text: Mature mRNA is always precisely co-linear to the gene from which it was transcribed

questions.why: In both bacteria and eukaryotes, transcription is initiated by RNA polymerase at a promoter. Promoter recognition uses different accessory factors in the two systems, but it positions the polymerase for initiation.

notes.A: A 5′ cap and a 3′ poly(A) tail are typical features of many eukaryotic mRNAs. Bacterial mRNAs do not routinely receive the same processing.
notes.B: Transcription and translation can be coupled in bacteria. In eukaryotic cells, nuclear transcription and cytoplasmic translation are generally separated.
notes.C: RNA polymerase synthesises RNA in the 5′-to-3′ direction while reading its template in the opposite direction.
notes.E: Eukaryotic RNA splicing can remove introns, so mature mRNA need not correspond continuously to the genomic sequence.

questions.stem: The first human protein produced through recombinant DNA technology is
questions.why: Somatostatin was reported in 1977 as an early demonstration of a human hormone produced through recombinant DNA technology. Recombinant insulin followed and became the first recombinant DNA-derived drug approved in the United States.

notes.A: Insulin was the landmark first approved recombinant DNA-derived therapeutic. The somatostatin research demonstration came earlier.
notes.B: Recombinant erythropoietin was developed later as a therapeutic protein and was not the first demonstration.
notes.C: Recombinant interferons were developed after the early somatostatin demonstration.
notes.E: Recombinant human growth hormone entered therapeutic use later and was not the earliest reported human protein in this comparison.

questions.stem: Some of the steps involved in Gene Cloning are given below: i) Insertion of isolated gene to the vector ii) Introduction of recombinant vector to the host iii) Isolation of desired gene iv) Expression of recombinant gene in host v) Extraction of recombinant gene product. The correct sequence of steps involved are
questions.why: The conceptual sequence in the question is to identify the gene of interest and have it carried by a vector before the host can express it. The expressed product must exist before it can be recovered.

notes.A: Expression in a host cannot precede the host's receipt of the gene-bearing vector in this description.
notes.C: The gene of interest must already have been identified or obtained before it can be carried by the vector.
notes.D: A vector cannot be called recombinant in this sequence until the gene of interest is part of it.

questions.stem:
Protein finger printing:
I. Resolves a mixture of peptides by electrophoretic separation in one direction only
II. Is a powerful method of comparing mixtures of peptides e.g. proteolytic digests of HbA and HbS
III. Separates mixtures of peptides first in a horizontal then in a vertical direction
questions.why: Classical peptide fingerprinting can compare digested proteins by separating their peptide fragments in two independent dimensions. A changed amino acid can alter one peptide's position, allowing maps of variants such as HbA and HbS to be compared.

notes.A: Classical two-dimensional peptide maps provide two axes of separation. The description limited to one direction is incomplete.
notes.B: Comparing digests of protein variants is a valid use. A two-dimensional fingerprint is not limited to a single electrophoretic direction.
notes.D: Separation in two dimensions is correct, but the first statement limits the process to one dimension and the comparison of peptide mixtures is also valid.
notes.E: The comparison and two-direction separation are appropriate. The assertion that there is only one separation direction does not fit the method.

questions.stem:
In eukaryotes, in order to initiate transcription
I. RNA strand must be present
II. RNA polymerase must be present
III. Core promoter sequence must be present
questions.why: Eukaryotic transcription initiation requires an RNA polymerase and a promoter context that can recruit the initiation machinery. The polymerase begins the RNA chain on its DNA template without needing a pre-existing RNA primer.

notes.A: Transcription does not require an existing RNA strand to start synthesis. The initiating nucleotides are joined by RNA polymerase.
notes.B: RNA polymerase is required, but the first statement incorrectly implies that an RNA primer must already be present.
notes.D: Core promoter elements help position the machinery. They do not imply a requirement for a pre-existing RNA strand.
notes.E: The polymerase and promoter statements fit initiation. The assertion that an RNA strand must already be present does not.

questions.stem:
Which one of the following statement is true regarding the DNA double helical structure?
I. The DNA double helix is coiled around a common axis known as the axis of symmetry
II. The hydrophilic deoxyribose-phosphate backbone of each chain is on the outside
III. The hydrophobic nitrogen bases are stacked inside.
questions.why: In the DNA double helix, two sugar–phosphate backbones wind about a common helical axis and are exposed to the aqueous environment. The bases pair and stack inside, where stacking interactions help stabilise the duplex.

notes.A: A common axis describes the shape, but the external backbones and internal stacking are also characteristic.
notes.B: The common axis and external backbones are correct. The alignment also places the stacked bases toward the inside.
notes.C: The positions of backbone and bases are correct. The two strands also share a common helical axis.
notes.D: The common axis and internal bases are correct. The polar sugar–phosphate backbones face outward.

questions.stem:
Telomeres are the repetitive sequence of Ts and G's... Which of the following are the properties of enzyme telomerase?
I. Telomerase is a reverse transcriptase enzyme
II. Telomerase consist of an RNA sequence that serves as a template
III. After completion of each cycle, telomerase translocates to 3'end of DNA to synthesize repetitive sequence
questions.why: Telomerase is a reverse transcriptase containing an RNA template. It extends a chromosome's DNA 3′ end with telomeric sequence, then realigns with the extended end so another repeat can be added.

notes.A: Reverse transcriptase activity is necessary, but the intrinsic RNA template and repeat-to-repeat realignment also define telomerase.
notes.B: The RNA template explains where the repeat information comes from. Moving or realigning to the extended end allows repeated rounds.
notes.C: The template and realignment are correct. The synthesis is carried out by an RNA-dependent DNA polymerase.
notes.D: Telomerase moves relative to the extended DNA end. The RNA within the enzyme is an essential part of this cycle.

questions.stem:
Which of the following is a characteristic feature of DNA replication?
I. DNA replication is template directed
II. DNA replication requires short RNA primers
III. DNA replication is a highly accurate process
questions.why: Chromosomal DNA replication uses parental DNA as the template and generally begins from short RNA-containing primers. Accurate base selection, polymerase proofreading and subsequent repair help make the overall process highly faithful.

notes.A: Template use is fundamental, but primer initiation and fidelity mechanisms are additional features.
notes.B: The template and primers explain how copying begins. Fidelity is also a characteristic of chromosomal replication.
notes.C: Primers and high accuracy are important, and the sequence is determined by a parental DNA template.
notes.D: Template-directed synthesis and high fidelity are correct. Replicative polymerases also need a primed end to extend.

questions.stem:
What is DNA replication?
I. Discontinuous
II. Non-conservative
III. Semi-conservative
questions.why: DNA replication is semiconservative because each daughter duplex receives one parental strand and one newly synthesised strand. At a typical fork it is semidiscontinuous, with a largely continuous leading strand and short fragments on the lagging strand.

notes.A: Lagging-strand synthesis is discontinuous. The distribution of parental strands into daughter duplexes is also a defining feature.
notes.B: Nonconservative copying is not the standard term. One original strand is retained in each daughter duplex.
notes.D: The process is semiconservative and includes discontinuous lagging-strand synthesis. Nonconservative does not describe the strand arrangement.
notes.E: Fragmented lagging-strand synthesis and semiconservative inheritance are correct. Adding nonconservative gives the wrong classification.

questions.stem:
During transcription in Eukaryotes RNA polymerase
I. binds directly to the promoter
II. needs sigma factor to first bind to promoter
III. need basal transcription factors first bind to promoter
questions.why: For typical eukaryotic RNA polymerase II transcription, general transcription factors assemble at the core promoter and recruit and position the polymerase. Sigma factors perform an analogous promoter-recognition role in many bacteria rather than in this eukaryotic system.

notes.A: Polymerase II ordinarily needs the general factors for efficient promoter recognition rather than binding and initiating there by itself.
notes.B: Sigma factors are associated with bacterial RNA polymerase, while eukaryotic polymerase II uses general transcription factors.
notes.D: This pairing gives the bacterial factor and omits the need for eukaryotic general transcription factors.
notes.E: General factors are needed in the standard model. Direct unaided promoter binding and use of a sigma factor do not fit that model.

questions.stem:
Aspartate transcarbamoylase (ATCase):
I. It may be allosterically inactivated after treatment with mercurials
II. It catalyzes the committed step of pyrimidine biosynthesis in prokaryotes
III. It catalyzes the committed step of pyrimidine biosynthesis in human beings
questions.why: ATCase is the committed step in bacteria. In humans, it's CPS II.

notes.A: Leaves out II, which is also true.
notes.C: Includes III, which is false, and leaves out I, which is true.
notes.D: Includes III, which is false, and leaves out II, which is true.
notes.E: Includes III, which is false.

questions.stem:
In the de novo synthesis of pyrimidine nucleotides:
I. the committed step is activated by ATP in prokaryotes
II. the committed step is inhibited by CTP in prokaryotes
III. the committed step is inhibited by UTP in human beings
questions.why: In the classical E. coli model, aspartate transcarbamylase is activated by ATP and inhibited by CTP. In human cells the comparable entry-point control is through the carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II domain of CAD, which is inhibited by UTP.

notes.A: ATP is a bacterial activator in the usual teaching model. CTP also inhibits the bacterial enzyme, and a distinct inhibitor acts in humans.
notes.B: ATP activates and CTP inhibits the classic bacterial enzyme, while UTP inhibits the entry step in human cells.
notes.C: CTP and UTP illustrate feedback in different systems. ATP is also an activator of the model bacterial enzyme.
notes.D: ATP activation in the bacterial model and UTP inhibition in humans are correct. The bacterial CTP feedback is also relevant.

questions.stem:
The main function of tRNA with regards to protein synthesis is
I. identifies amino acids and transports them to ribosomes
II. Proof-reading
III. Inhibits protein synthesis
questions.why: A tRNA carries an amino acid to the ribosome and uses its anticodon to recognise an mRNA codon. Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases establish which amino acid is attached, and fidelity mechanisms check charging and codon pairing.

notes.B: Carrying amino acids is the adaptor function. Proofreading is chiefly performed by the charging enzymes and ribosomal selection machinery.
notes.C: Proofreading is a separate fidelity process, and inhibition is not the normal purpose of aminoacyl-tRNA.
notes.D: Transfer RNA supports elongation by supplying amino acids. It is not normally an inhibitor of protein synthesis.
notes.E: The adaptor function is correct. Proofreading and inhibition are not its principal biological roles.

questions.stem: The following are true except:

options.label: A
options.text: Recombinant bacterial colonies can also be identified by applying a polymerase chain reaction using the bacterial colonies as templates.

options.label: B
options.text: The presence of the insert in the plasmid constructs can also be assessed via restriction endonuclease digest of the isolated plasmids.

options.label: C
options.text: The presence of the insert in the plasmid constructs can also be assessed via sequencing of the affected region.

options.label: D
options.text: Biotechnology is a big part of industry.

questions.why: Gene therapy can be limited by delivery, durability, immune responses, safety and access. The other choices describe conceptual ways a DNA construct may be checked or the broader role of biotechnology.

notes.A: A PCR-based check can indicate whether a colony carries a DNA region of interest. It does not remove the limitations of gene therapy.
notes.B: A restriction digest can provide an expected size pattern for a DNA construct, which is a standard concept in verifying its structure.
notes.C: Sequence information can verify the identity of an insert and its boundaries. This is a valid form of construct verification.
notes.D: Biotechnology has applications in medicine, agriculture and manufacturing, so its industrial importance is not the false claim.

questions.stem:
Concerning protein structure:
I. Primary structure is when the protein only has one polypeptide chain
II. An example of secondary structure of a protein is α-helix
III. Primary structure is the sequence of amino acids in a protein
questions.why: Primary structure is the amino acid sequence of a polypeptide. Secondary structure describes recurrent local backbone conformations such as the alpha helix. Proteins with more than one chain still have primary sequences for their subunits.

notes.A: The number of chains concerns quaternary organisation. It does not define primary structure.
notes.B: An alpha helix is a valid secondary structure example, but the statement restricting primary structure to single-chain proteins is incorrect.
notes.D: Amino acid sequence defines primary structure. The claim that primary structure requires just one chain is incorrect.
notes.E: The sequence and alpha-helix statements are accurate. Adding the single-chain restriction makes the grouping false.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Increases in alanine transaminase in blood are indicative of kidney damage.
Reason: increases in alanine transaminase in blood results from kidney damage.
questions.why: An increase in serum alanine aminotransferase most often points to hepatocellular injury. ALT is not a standard marker of kidney damage. Kidney assessment usually draws on measures such as creatinine-based filtration estimates and urine findings.

notes.A: Both statements assign ALT to the wrong diagnostic context. Its standard use is to help evaluate liver-cell injury.
notes.B: There are not two true claims here. Elevated ALT is not a characteristic indicator of renal injury.
notes.C: The assertion is false because ALT is principally used in the evaluation of hepatocellular damage.
notes.D: Kidney damage is not the usual reason for a raised ALT, making the stated explanation inaccurate.

questions.stem:
Assertion: The Lineweaver-Burk plot makes it difficult to calculate Km and Vmax of a reaction.
Reason: the Lineweaver-Burk plot gives a straight line.
questions.why: The Lineweaver–Burk plot graphs reciprocal velocity against reciprocal substrate concentration. For ideal Michaelis–Menten data it gives a straight line, with intercepts that can be used to estimate the kinetic constants. In real data, the transform can amplify error at low substrate concentrations.

notes.A: The straight-line transformation is real, but it was introduced to make the intercepts easier to estimate from ideal data.
notes.B: The reason correctly identifies the linear relation. The assertion does not describe the usual purpose of that transformation.
notes.C: The plot does produce a straight line for ideal data, so the reason should not be marked false.
notes.E: The linear relationship is valid in the model even though fitting untransformed data is often more reliable in practice.

questions.stem: Translation with mRNA codon: Find the tRNA anticodon. (Given mRNA codon: 5'-AUG-3')
questions.why: The anticodon pairs antiparallel to the mRNA codon. With the codon written 5′-AUG-3′, the complementary RNA sequence is 3′-UAC-5′, or 5′-CAU-3′ if the anticodon is written in its own 5′-to-3′ direction.

notes.B: Transfer RNA uses uracil rather than thymine. The specified orientation must also be opposite to the aligned codon.
notes.C: UAC is the aligned complement only when written 3′ to 5′ against the codon. Reversing its end labels changes the molecule described.
notes.D: The end labels are antiparallel, but thymine is not the base used at that position in the usual RNA anticodon.

questions.stem: A DNA template strand reads 5'-ATG-3'. What is its RNA transcript?
questions.why: RNA polymerase reads the DNA template in the 3′-to-5′ direction. For this written template, the RNA is complementary and antiparallel. Written in the usual 5′-to-3′ direction, it is 5′-CAU-3′.

notes.B: AUG would correspond to an ATG coding strand. Here the given sequence is explicitly the template strand.
notes.C: UAC is the aligned complement from left to right, but in that alignment its direction is 3′ to 5′, not 5′ to 3′.
notes.D: The proposed strand contains thymine. RNA uses uracil in the usual complement to adenine.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Antibodies can prevent against virus reinfection.
Reason: antibodies produced to the viral receptor can block the viral binding to host cells.
questions.why: Neutralizing antibodies bind to viral surface proteins and prevent attachment to host cells.

notes.B: Wrong here: the reason does explain the assertion.
notes.C: Wrong here: the reason is true.
notes.D: Wrong here: the assertion is true.
notes.E: Wrong here: the assertion is true and the reason is true.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Antibodies are crucial once a viral infection is established.
Reason: antibodies can eliminate the virus even when the viral genome is integrated into the host cell.
questions.why: Once integrated, antibodies cannot reach or eliminate the virus.

notes.A: Wrong here: the assertion is false and the reason is false.
notes.B: Wrong here: the assertion is false and the reason is false.
notes.C: Wrong here: the assertion is false.
notes.D: Wrong here: the reason is false.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Cell-mediated immune response is the main protective response against extracellular bacteria.
Reason: Cell-mediated immune response causes inactivation of bacteria toxin.
questions.why: Antibodies and complement are major means of protection against extracellular bacteria. They can neutralise toxins and promote bacterial clearance by phagocytes. T cells help organise some of these responses, but direct toxin neutralisation is usually antibody mediated.

notes.A: Neither claim describes the usual primary mechanism. Antibodies can neutralise extracellular toxins and promote bacterial removal.
notes.B: The overall division of labour and the claim of direct cell-mediated toxin inactivation are both inaccurate.
notes.C: The assertion is incorrect as a general rule because extracellular bacteria are major targets of humoral immunity.
notes.D: Neutralising many bacterial toxins directly is a role of antibodies rather than of the cell-mediated response.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Cytokines can be pleiotropic.
Reason: cytokines of different types can have the same effect on the same cell.
questions.why: Pleiotropy means one cytokine has multiple effects. Different cytokines having the same effect is redundancy.

notes.A: Wrong here: the reason is false.
notes.B: Wrong here: the reason is false.
notes.D: Wrong here: the assertion is true and the reason is false.
notes.E: Wrong here: the assertion is true.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Cytokines can stimulate the production of other cytokines.
Reason: cytokines can cause a cascading effect.
questions.why: A cytokine cascade occurs when an initial signal induces responding cells to produce additional cytokines. The secondary mediators can then recruit more cells or change their activity, expanding the original response.

notes.B: Induction of additional cytokines is what makes the response a cascade, so the two statements describe the same linked process.
notes.C: A cascading response is an established feature of cytokine signalling and can involve induction of further cytokines.
notes.D: The assertion is supported because a cell can respond to one cytokine by releasing others.
notes.E: Both statements describe how a primary cytokine signal can lead to a sequence of secondary responses.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Chemokines are a family of chemoattractant cytokines.
Reason: chemokines regulate lymphoid organ development and T-cell differentiation.
questions.why: Chemokines are a family of cytokines that guide cell migration. In addition to immediate recruitment, some help organise lymphoid tissues or position developing and mature T cells, which can influence differentiation and behaviour.

notes.A: Roles in tissue organisation are valid, but they are broader consequences of chemokine signalling rather than the definition of a chemoattractant.
notes.C: Chemokines can contribute to lymphoid organisation and T-cell development by directing where cells migrate and interact.
notes.D: The assertion is correct because directed cell migration is a defining action of chemokines.
notes.E: Both statements describe recognised chemokine biology, with the reason addressing wider roles beyond the definition.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Cell-mediated immune response is the main protective response against intracellular organisms.
Reason: Cell-mediated immune response causes inactivation of bacteria toxin.
questions.why: T-cell-mediated immunity is especially important against organisms within host cells. Helper T cells can activate macrophages, and cytotoxic T cells can remove infected cells. Neutralisation of soluble bacterial toxins is ordinarily an antibody function.

notes.A: The assertion is generally correct. The reason assigns direct toxin neutralisation to the wrong arm of adaptive immunity.
notes.B: Toxin neutralisation is not an additional true statement about the primary cell-mediated mechanism.
notes.D: Cell-mediated responses are important against intracellular organisms. The toxin explanation does not describe that role.
notes.E: The assertion is supported even though the reason is inaccurate. Intracellular targets require responses directed at infected cells.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Adaptive immunity is the first line of defense against viral infections.
Reason: adaptive immunity results in the production of antibodies that block viral infections by preventing viral binding to host cells.
questions.why: Innate defences, including barriers and rapid antiviral responses, act before a new adaptive response develops. Adaptive antibodies can later neutralise extracellular viral particles by blocking attachment or entry.

notes.A: Antibody production is part of adaptive immunity, but it is not the first newly activated line of defence during an initial infection.
notes.B: The reason is valid, whereas the assertion incorrectly places a newly generated adaptive response before innate protection.
notes.C: Adaptive antibodies can block an early step in infection of cells. The claim that adaptive immunity is the body's first line is false.
notes.E: The assertion is inaccurate, but neutralisation by adaptive antibodies is a recognised mechanism.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Antibodies have an important role in containing the spread of a virus in the acute phase of the infection.
Reason: antibodies can eliminate established infections even when the viral genome is integrated into the host chromosomal DNA.
questions.why: Neutralising antibodies can bind extracellular viral particles and help limit spread to other cells during acute infection. They do not remove viral genetic material that has become integrated in a host cell.

notes.A: The acute containment role is valid, but antibodies cannot directly eradicate a genome integrated into host DNA.
notes.B: Both statements cannot be accepted because extracellular neutralisation does not excise an intracellular integrated genome.
notes.D: The assertion is true. The reason confuses limiting spread with removing genetic material already present inside host cells.
notes.E: Antibodies can contribute to containment during acute infection even though the proposed mechanism of eliminating integration is wrong.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Sporozoites initiate the major symptoms in malaria.
Reason: sporozoites migrate to the liver where they infect hepatocytes, after which the parasite develops into a multinucleate liver stage (schizont).
questions.why: The main clinical symptoms of malaria generally reflect the blood stage, when parasites multiply in red blood cells and trigger inflammatory responses. An earlier stage develops in the liver and is often clinically silent.

notes.A: Liver stage development occurs, but it is not the principal cause of the characteristic fever and other major symptoms.
notes.B: The reason is true while the assertion attributes the main symptoms to the wrong stage.
notes.C: The main symptomatic phase is the blood stage. The stated early liver stage is real.
notes.E: The assertion is inaccurate, but the reason correctly identifies development in hepatocytes before the symptomatic phase.

questions.stem: Cytokines can be redundant when

options.label: A
options.text: The cytokine has no effect on the cell it acts on

options.label: B
options.text: Cytokine acts on a distant cell

options.label: C
options.text: different cytokines have the same effects

options.label: D
options.text: One cytokine can have different effects on different cells

questions.why: Cytokine redundancy means that different cytokines can produce overlapping effects on a responding cell. It contrasts with pleiotropy, in which one cytokine can have several effects or act on different cell types.

notes.A: A lack of response can result from absent receptors or other factors. Redundancy requires overlapping actions from distinct cytokines.
notes.B: Action at a distant site describes endocrine signalling rather than redundancy between cytokines.
notes.D: Multiple effects from one cytokine describe pleiotropy. Redundancy concerns similar effects from more than one cytokine.

questions.stem: When a TNF produced by an T helper cell acts on a macrophage to produce IL-1 and TNF, this effect is described as
questions.why: A cytokine cascade is a sequence in which one mediator causes a responding cell to release additional cytokines. Here a TNF signal prompts macrophages to produce IL-1 and further TNF.

notes.A: Synergy means signals acting together have a stronger combined effect. The example instead describes a signal inducing more mediators.
notes.C: Redundancy means that different mediators produce a similar effect. It does not describe sequential amplification by release of more cytokines.
notes.D: Pleiotropy is the ability of one mediator to affect different cells or processes. The defining feature here is induction of another wave of cytokines.

questions.stem: Bacteria growing within macrophages are killed by:

options.label: A
options.text: Directly by cytokines released from Th1 cells.

questions.why: Activated macrophages can use reactive oxygen and nitrogen species as part of their intracellular antimicrobial defences. Signals from helper T cells can enhance macrophage activity, but the macrophage generates the effector molecules.

notes.A: Helper T-cell cytokines activate or strengthen macrophage responses. They are not generally the direct chemical agents killing bacteria inside phagosomes.
notes.B: Antibodies can coat extracellular bacteria, but they do not directly supply the main intracellular killing mechanism in activated macrophages.
notes.C: Cytotoxic T cells can remove infected host cells. The question instead asks what kills bacteria within the macrophage.

questions.stem: An exotoxin is the only significant virulence factor and is responsible for all the symptoms of the disease in
questions.why: Diphtheria is primarily a toxemia.

notes.B: Shigella dysentery involves invasion of the gut lining, not just a toxin.
notes.C: TB damage comes from intracellular growth and the host response.
notes.D: Strep throat involves invasion and several virulence factors.

questions.stem: Mycobacterium tuberculosis bacteria avoid innate immunity by

options.label: D
options.text: Living in an immuno-privileged tissue site

questions.why: Macrophages normally move engulfed material through vesicles that mature and fuse with lysosomes, where degradative processes support killing. A block in that maturation or fusion step reduces clearance of the engulfed bacterium.

notes.B: A capsule can reduce uptake of some other bacteria. The mechanism the question is testing concerns the processing of material after engulfment.
notes.C: Complement can help mark extracellular microbes for clearance. The particular interaction tested here is within the macrophage vesicle.
notes.D: An immune-privileged site is a tissue context. This question concerns survival after uptake by a phagocytic cell.

questions.stem: Extracellular bacteria are optimally killed by:
questions.why: Antibodies and complement can coat extracellular bacteria with molecules recognised by phagocytes. Macrophages can then engulf and degrade the marked bacteria. Complement can also directly damage some susceptible bacterial membranes.

notes.A: Macrophages can ingest bacteria alone, but antibody and complement opsonisation can make recognition and uptake more efficient.
notes.B: Complement helps mark some bacteria and may lyse susceptible species. Phagocytes provide an additional route for removal.
notes.C: Antibodies can neutralise or coat bacteria. Complement and phagocytes often act alongside them to clear the organism more effectively.

questions.stem: The inappropriate response of immune system towards a relatively harmless antigen causing harm to the host is referred as
questions.why: Hypersensitivity is an immune response that causes tissue injury or symptoms rather than a proportionate protective response. Allergy to a relatively harmless environmental substance is one familiar example.

notes.B: Autoimmunity is directed against self antigens. A harmful response to an otherwise innocuous external antigen is more generally a hypersensitivity reaction.
notes.C: Immunodeficiency is impaired immune protection, rather than excessive or damaging reactivity to an antigen.
notes.D: Tolerance means antigen-specific unresponsiveness. It prevents responses rather than describing the harmful response in this question.

questions.stem: Which of the following Ig is involved in mediating allergic reactions
questions.why: Immediate allergic reactions commonly involve IgE bound to high-affinity receptors on mast cells and basophils. An allergen can cross-link these surface-bound antibodies and trigger mediator release.

notes.A: IgG contributes to some hypersensitivity reactions, but it is not the main antibody class in classic immediate allergy.
notes.B: IgM is prominent early in many primary responses and can activate complement. Immediate allergy chiefly involves IgE.
notes.D: IgA is important in mucosal secretions and helps defend surfaces. It is not the typical mediator of mast-cell immediate allergy.

questions.stem: ___ is a state of unresponsiveness of the immune system to a potential immunogen
questions.why: Immune tolerance is antigen-specific unresponsiveness despite the ability to respond to other stimuli. Tolerance to self antigens helps prevent autoimmune disease.

notes.A: Autoimmunity is an immune response against self. It can result when relevant self-tolerance mechanisms fail.
notes.B: Immunodeficiency generally refers to impaired immune function, not unresponsiveness to one defined antigen with other responses intact.
notes.D: Recognition can occur without a harmful response. The state of antigen-specific unresponsiveness is called tolerance.

questions.stem: The major chemical messenger involved in hypersensitivity is
questions.why: Histamine is the primary mediator of immediate hypersensitivity.

notes.A: Interleukins are signalling cytokines, not the main hypersensitivity mediator.
notes.C: Interferons are antiviral.
notes.D: Lysosomes are organelles, not messengers.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a cell mediated hypersensitivity reaction?
questions.why: Type IV hypersensitivity is mediated by sensitised T cells. They can activate inflammatory cells or directly injure target cells. The reaction is often delayed compared with immediate IgE-mediated allergy.

notes.A: Type I reactions are usually immediate and involve IgE-dependent mast-cell or basophil activation.
notes.B: Type II reactions involve antibodies against cell-associated antigens or receptors rather than a chiefly T-cell-mediated mechanism.
notes.C: Type III reactions arise from immune complexes depositing in tissues and activating inflammatory pathways.

questions.stem: The inability to distinguish self-cells from none-self cells may lead to
questions.why: Autoimmune disease can arise when immune tolerance to self fails and lymphocytes or their products attack the body's own cells and tissues. This differs from an inadequate response to infection.

notes.A: Hypersensitivity is a broad term for damaging immune reactions and can involve external antigens. A response specifically directed at self is autoimmune.
notes.C: Immunodeficiency impairs defence. Losing the distinction between self and non-self instead risks inappropriate attack on the body's tissues.
notes.D: Tolerance is a mechanism that normally limits responses to self antigens. Its failure can contribute to autoimmunity.

questions.stem: Majority of auto immune diseases are
questions.why: Many autoimmune diseases are driven by autoantibodies.

notes.A: Some are T-cell mediated (e.g. type 1 diabetes), but most involve autoantibodies.
notes.C: Macrophages are effectors, not the main driver.
notes.D: Mast cells drive allergy.

questions.stem: All of the following are autoimmune diseases except
questions.why: Severe combined immunodeficiency is a disorder of impaired lymphocyte development or function. The hallmark is inadequate immune protection. Rheumatoid arthritis, Graves disease and autoimmune adrenal insufficiency involve inappropriate responses to self tissues.

notes.A: Rheumatoid arthritis is an immune-mediated inflammatory disease that commonly affects joints. It is classified as autoimmune.
notes.C: Graves disease involves autoantibodies that stimulate the thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor.
notes.D: Autoimmune destruction of the adrenal cortex is a common cause of Addison disease. Other causes of primary adrenal insufficiency also exist.

questions.stem: Type I hypersensitivity require which of the following initial priming events to occur?
questions.why: Type I hypersensitivity typically begins with sensitisation. The initial exposure induces allergen-specific IgE, which binds mast-cell and basophil receptors. Later exposure can cross-link that IgE and trigger release of mediators.

notes.B: A later response can produce symptoms, but allergen-specific IgE normally has to be generated during sensitisation first.
notes.C: Cellular injury is not the required immune priming event. Priming is the development of allergen-specific IgE.
notes.D: Degranulation is a downstream event that occurs after an allergen cross-links IgE on a sensitised cell.

questions.stem: Immune modulatory mechanisms employed by pathogens to evade host immune response could include
questions.why: Some pathogens induce tolerance to avoid being attacked.

notes.A: Autoimmunity is a host disorder, not a pathogen strategy.
notes.B: Phagolysosome fusion KILLS pathogens; they try to block it.
notes.D: ROS are host weapons.

questions.stem: Type II hypersensitivity reactions are characterized by
questions.why: Type II hypersensitivity is mediated by antibodies, usually IgG or IgM, directed against cell-associated antigens or receptors. The antibodies can cause cell injury through immune effectors or alter receptor function.

notes.B: Mast-cell degranulation is characteristic of immediate type I hypersensitivity rather than the defining type II mechanism.
notes.C: Erythrocytes can be targets of type II reactions, as in some transfusion reactions. They are not involved as the defining effector in every type II reaction.
notes.D: Histamine is a major early mediator of immediate allergy. Antibody binding to a cell-associated antigen defines type II.

questions.stem: Tumor antigens are ___ that are inappropriately expressed and found on abnormal cells
questions.why: Tumor antigens are often overexpressed self-proteins.

notes.B: Most tumour antigens are altered or overexpressed self-proteins.
notes.C: Antibodies recognise antigens; they are not antigens.
notes.D: T cell receptors recognise antigens.

questions.stem: Cancer results when a mutation leads to which of the following?

options.label: D
options.text: Shut down of the cell cycle

questions.why: Cancer can develop as genetic changes weaken controls on division, survival and tissue invasion. Loss of cell-cycle control can allow abnormal cells to continue proliferating when normal growth signals would stop them.

notes.A: Death of a damaged cell usually limits expansion of that cell. Cancer depends on survival and outgrowth of abnormal cells.
notes.B: Apoptosis is regulated cell death and can prevent damaged cells from expanding. Resistance to apoptosis can contribute to cancer.
notes.D: Cell-cycle arrest prevents further division. Cancer involves failure or evasion of controls that would normally impose arrest.

questions.stem: When allergen crosslinks with IgE bound to the Fc receptor on the mast cells... Which of the following receptor have high affinity towards IgE?
questions.why: FcεRI is the high-affinity receptor for the Fc portion of IgE on mast cells and basophils. When a multivalent allergen cross-links receptor-bound IgE, intracellular signalling can trigger degranulation.

notes.B: FcεRII, also called CD23, is the lower-affinity IgE receptor. It is distinct from the high-affinity mast-cell receptor.
notes.C: Membrane immunoglobulin serves as an antigen receptor on B cells. It is not the mast-cell receptor that binds the Fc region of IgE.
notes.D: T-cell receptors recognise antigens in an appropriate presenting context. They do not hold IgE on mast cells.

questions.stem: A hereditary predisposition of the development of immediate hypersensitivity reaction against common environmental antigens are called
questions.why: Atopy is a personal or familial predisposition to develop IgE responses to common environmental allergens. It increases the likelihood of immediate allergic conditions such as allergic rhinitis or allergic asthma.

notes.A: Atrophy refers to a decrease in cell or tissue size. It does not describe inherited susceptibility to allergy.
notes.C: Anergy is functional unresponsiveness of an immune cell, rather than an increased tendency to develop an allergic response.
notes.D: Synergy occurs when combined signals produce a greater effect together. It is not the name for a familial predisposition to immediate allergy.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not an example of Type I hypersensitivity reaction?
questions.why: Systemic lupus erythematosus is an autoimmune disease in which immune complex-mediated injury is a classic mechanism. Immediate IgE-mediated reactions contribute to allergic rhinitis and allergic forms of asthma and atopic disease.

notes.A: Allergic asthma can involve allergen-specific IgE and mast-cell mediators, although not all asthma is allergic.
notes.B: Allergic rhinitis is a classic immediate hypersensitivity condition triggered by common airborne allergens.
notes.D: Atopic dermatitis has several mechanisms, including skin-barrier dysfunction and inflammation. IgE-associated atopy can be part of its presentation.

questions.stem: During a blood transfusion, ABO incompatibilities... Which of the following antibody isotype is primarily involved in this type II hypersensitivity reaction?
questions.why: Naturally occurring ABO isohaemagglutinins are often IgM. In an incompatible transfusion, they can activate complement on donor red cells and cause rapid haemolysis. IgG ABO antibodies can also occur, particularly in group O individuals.

notes.A: IgG contributes to several red-cell immune reactions and can be present in the ABO system, but IgM is the usual teaching answer for acute ABO incompatibility.
notes.C: IgA provides mucosal protection and is not the principal isotype responsible for classic ABO red-cell haemolysis.
notes.D: IgE mediates many immediate allergies and is not the predominant ABO antibody in this reaction.

questions.stem: Which of the following cytokines are important for DTH and also used of diagnosis of Mycobacterium tuberculosis?
questions.why: Interferon gamma supports cell-mediated immunity and macrophage activation in delayed hypersensitivity. Interferon gamma release assays detect a memory T-cell response that can support a diagnosis of tuberculosis infection. The result alone does not distinguish latent infection from active disease.

notes.A: TNF alpha contributes to inflammation and granuloma biology but is not the interferon measured by the named class of tests.
notes.B: TNF beta, also called lymphotoxin alpha, has immune signalling roles but is not the usual readout for these assays.
notes.C: Interferon alpha is a type I interferon with prominent antiviral roles. These assays instead measure the response involving interferon gamma.

questions.stem: Placental tissue is able to evade immune surveillance via
questions.why: Trophoblast cells downregulate classical MHC class I molecules.

notes.B: This helps, but the main mechanism is MHC downregulation.
notes.C: Autoimmunity would harm, not protect.
notes.D: Regulatory T cells are ENHANCED, not exacerbated, and that is not the main evasion route.

questions.stem: A break in tolerance to microbiome could lead to
questions.why: Ulcerative colitis is a form of inflammatory bowel disease in which an inappropriate response to intestinal microbes may contribute to inflammation. Host genetics, the mucosal barrier and environmental factors also influence disease.

notes.B: Many peptic ulcers are associated with Helicobacter pylori or anti-inflammatory drug use. They are not the classic example of a failure of tolerance to the colonic microbiome.
notes.C: Vomiting is a nonspecific reflex symptom. It does not identify the chronic mucosal inflammation described here.
notes.D: Bronchoconstriction can occur in airway disease and allergy, rather than being the expected manifestation of chronic immune dysregulation in the colon.

questions.stem: Autoimmunity is mostly treated with
questions.why: Corticosteroids can suppress inflammatory gene expression and are used to control inflammation in many autoimmune diseases, particularly during flares. Long-term treatment is disease-specific and may rely on other immunomodulatory therapies.

notes.A: Vaccines generally prepare protective immunity against infection. They are not the usual general anti-inflammatory treatment for established autoimmunity.
notes.B: Allergen desensitisation can treat selected allergies. It is not a general treatment for immune responses directed against self.
notes.C: Antihistamines can alleviate some immediate allergic symptoms but generally do not control the underlying inflammation of autoimmune disease.

questions.stem: True or false: Autoimmunity results when the immune system over reacts.
questions.why: Autoimmunity involves an immune response directed at self antigens because self-tolerance has failed. An excessive response to a foreign but harmless antigen, such as pollen, can instead cause allergy.

notes.A: An overreaction alone is not sufficient to define autoimmunity. The immune response must be directed against components of the host.

questions.stem: True or false: Autoimmunity affects women above 50 years.
questions.why: They frequently affect younger women (e.g., SLE in the 20s and 30s).

questions.stem: True or false: Anergy is a mechanism by which the immune cell induces tolerance.
questions.why: Anergy is a state of functional unresponsiveness. In the periphery, a lymphocyte that recognises antigen without the necessary co-stimulatory signals can become anergic and fail to mount a response to that antigen.

notes.B: Anergy is one established route to peripheral tolerance, alongside deletion of some lymphocytes and suppression by regulatory cells.

questions.stem: True or false: Central tolerance occurs in thymus and bone marrow.
questions.why: Central tolerance develops while lymphocytes mature. T cells encounter self antigens in the thymus, and B cells undergo tolerance checks in the bone marrow. Outcomes can include deletion, receptor editing or regulatory differentiation, depending on the cell.

notes.B: The thymus and bone marrow are the main sites of early tolerance checks for developing T cells and B cells, respectively.

questions.stem: True or false: Apoptosis is a common mechanism of inducing peripheral tolerance.
questions.why: Peripheral tolerance can include deletion of mature self-reactive lymphocytes by apoptosis. Persistent or inappropriate antigen recognition can trigger death signals, while anergy and regulatory suppression provide other means of limiting responses.

notes.B: Programmed death can remove self-reactive cells outside the primary lymphoid organs and thereby contribute to tolerance.

questions.stem: True or false: Some drugs and chemical agents can cause autoimmunity.
questions.why: Some medications or other agents can trigger an autoimmune syndrome or promote autoantibody formation in susceptible individuals. The mechanism depends on the exposure and can involve altered immune regulation or recognition.

notes.B: Drug-induced autoimmune syndromes demonstrate that an external chemical exposure can contribute to loss of normal tolerance.

questions.stem: True or false: Histamines are formed by covalent reduction of histidine.
questions.why: Histamine is formed by decarboxylation of histidine. Histidine decarboxylase removes the carboxyl group as carbon dioxide, leaving the corresponding biogenic amine.

notes.A: The key reaction removes carbon dioxide from histidine. It is decarboxylation rather than a reduction.

questions.stem: During hypersensitivity skin test a patient received an allergen subcutaneously, after which the patient developed skin redness, edema, and pain due to histamine action. This biogenic amine is produced as the result of the following transformation of histidine amino acid:
questions.why: Histidine decarboxylase removes the alpha-carboxyl group of histidine to form histamine. Released histamine can dilate vessels and increase vascular permeability, contributing to redness and swelling in an immediate skin reaction.

notes.B: Adding a methyl group does not make histamine from histidine. Methylation can instead occur during histamine metabolism.
notes.C: Phosphorylation adds a phosphate group and would not produce the biogenic amine in this reaction.
notes.D: Isomerisation rearranges atoms without the loss of carbon dioxide needed to convert histidine to histamine.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Vitiligo and albinism are diseases affecting the skin.
Reason: Vitiligo and albinism are inheritable.
questions.why: The assertion is true: both affect skin pigmentation. The reason is false as stated: albinism is inherited, but vitiligo is an acquired autoimmune loss of melanocytes (genes only raise susceptibility).

notes.A: Wrong here: the reason is false.
notes.B: Wrong here: the reason is false.
notes.D: Wrong here: the assertion is true and the reason is false.
notes.E: Wrong here: the assertion is true.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Tryptophan is involved in the synthesis of serotonin.
Reason: Tryptophan is a precursor to the neurotransmitter dopamine.
questions.why: Tryptophan is converted to 5-hydroxytryptophan and then to serotonin. Dopamine is made through a different pathway, in which tyrosine is converted to L-DOPA and then decarboxylated.

notes.A: The serotonin assertion is true, but the reason is false because dopamine is derived from tyrosine rather than tryptophan.
notes.B: Both claims cannot be true. Tryptophan feeds serotonin synthesis, whereas tyrosine feeds catecholamine synthesis.
notes.D: Tryptophan is a serotonin precursor, so the assertion should not be marked false.
notes.E: The reason is inaccurate, but the stated relationship between tryptophan and serotonin is well established.

questions.stem: A patient with cancer of the urinary bladder has high rates of serotonin and hydroxyanthranilic acid. It is caused by excess of which amino acid?
questions.why: Tryptophan is the precursor for serotonin. Its degradation via the kynurenine pathway produces hydroxyanthranilic acid.

notes.B: Histidine gives histamine.
notes.C: Methionine gives SAM and homocysteine.
notes.D: Tyrosine gives catecholamines and melanin.

questions.stem:
What is likely to be the complications exhibited by a child with severe combined immunodeficiency:
I. Infection from vaccination
II. Severe cases of yeast infection
III. Comparatively susceptible to infection compared to siblings.
questions.why: Severe combined immunodeficiency causes a profound defect in adaptive immune function. Affected infants are vulnerable to serious or recurrent infections, including fungal infections, and some live vaccines can cause disease in a severely immunocompromised child.

notes.A: Complications from certain live vaccines are possible, and fungal or other severe infections also reflect the immune defect.
notes.B: Live vaccine-associated infection and severe yeast infection are possible. Susceptibility to a broad range of infections is also increased.
notes.C: Fungal infections and general susceptibility are characteristic. Severe immune impairment can also allow disease from certain live vaccines.
notes.D: Complications can follow certain live vaccines, and overall susceptibility is increased. Persistent or severe yeast infection is another recognised finding.
